Family history research · New Brunswick

Were the Eatmons Black Loyalists?

You asked for pictures, references, and news articles on the Eatmon family and a possible Black Loyalist connection — and flagged that Chester Eatmon is “in the news.” Here is everything the research found, with the two family lines kept strictly separate.

Research gathered 11 November 2026. Surname note: sources use Eatmon and Eatman for the same family — even for the same person — so both spellings were searched throughout. Military records consistently use Eatman; Eatmon is the family variant, and Eldridge also appears as Eastman.

Added for Remembrance Day, 11 November 2026: a full section on the family’s military service (§6) — who served, who was killed, and what Ancestry does and does not add.

Added 11 November 2026 (§7): findings from a read of your own Ancestry account — your direct Eatmon line (Chester is your great-grandfather), your AncestryDNA origins and matches, and the military records Ancestry’s index holds. A second, deeper Ancestry dig the same day added Chester’s 1986 Windsor Star story (§4), two marriage certificates in full, Major Eatmon’s 1911 census household, Find a Grave family bios, an explicit list of what stays locked behind Ancestry membership, and the tree’s data-quality flags (§7).

Updated 11 November 2026 (§6): a follow-up pass on the military gaps — Manzer Eatman’s attestation paper read in full at Library and Archives Canada, new index records for Joseph and Mansfield Eatmon, a second source for Dubert Eatman, a Korea check, and the “Mrs Hannah Eatmon” question resolved as far as the records allow. Conflicts and unproven leads are flagged, not smoothed over.

The short answer

No Eatmon or Eatman has been found in the Book of Negroes. The Eatmons are not documented as 1783 Black Loyalists under that name.

That is not the whole story, though. The famous Black Loyalist ancestor in the best-known Eatmon-connected family is real — he is just on the other side of the family. And the Eatmons themselves belong to Elm Hill, a Black Loyalist settlement, which is likely where the connection comes from.

✓ 1783 record found

The Gosman / Goseman line — paternal

John Goseman is in the Book of Negroes (Library and Archives Canada, item 905), sailing on the brig Concord in 1783. He is the 4× great-grandfather of soprano Measha Brueggergosman-Lee — through her father, Sterling Gosman.

No 1783 entry found

The Eatmon line — maternal

Measha’s mother is Anne (Ann) Eatmon, daughter of Chester Eatmon of Elm Hill and Fredericton. No source found names an Eatmon as a 1783 entrant — the Eatmon link is to the Elm Hill Black Loyalist community, not to a named 1783 record.

1 · The Book of Negroes check

The Book of Negroes records about 3,000 Black refugees who sailed from New York to Nova Scotia between 23 April and 30 November 1783. Nova Scotia Archives hosts the record; Library and Archives Canada (LAC) says its database holds 2,831 references — one for every person listed.

Searches for “Eatmon” and “Eatman” against the Book of Negroes — including site-restricted searches of the LAC database — returned no matching entrant. The only pages those searches surface are about Measha Brueggergosman-Lee, where Eatmon is her mother’s surname and the Book of Negroes ancestor is a Gosman (see §2).

How solid is “not found”? Confidence is medium, and the research is upfront about why: the conclusion rests on indexed searches of the LAC database and web searches returning no hit — not on a page-by-page reading of all 2,831 entries or the manuscript itself. A live attempt to drive the LAC and Nova Scotia Archives search interfaces failed in this run (the LAC search page would not load). About 800 entrants in the Book have no recorded surname at all, so a first-name-only Eatmon ancestor could not have been ruled out this way.

Spellings to keep trying

Eatmon and Eatman are variants of one New Brunswick family name. Chester Eatmon was born to “William Bateman Eatman” and changed his surname to Eatmon after marrying Edna. Census records for the same Elm Hill woman appear as both “Elisabeth Eatmon” (1881) and “Lizzie Eatman” (1891). Measha’s mother is “Anne Eatmon” in Wikipedia but “Anne Eatman” in the UEL blog. Any future archive search should also try Eastman, Easmon, and Edman.

Do not conflate Easmon: the Sierra Leone Easmon family (William Easmon, Freetown settler, 11 March 1792) is a different surname, described as a variation of Eastman/Eastmond. No Eatmon was found in Sierra Leone settler records. See Wikipedia — Easmon family.

2 · The actual 1783 ancestor: John Goseman

In 2007, soprano Measha Brueggergosman-Lee (née Gosman, born 28 June 1977, Fredericton) traced her family on CBC’s Who Do You Think You Are? and learned her paternal 4× great-grandparents were John Gosman and his wife Rose — African Americans who each escaped slavery in New England during the American Revolution by going to British lines. John was from Connecticut, Rose from Rhode Island. They were recorded in the Book of Negroes with their baby daughter Fanny, born free in British lines, and sailed in 1783 on one of the last ships to leave New York for Nova Scotia.

Measha Brueggergosman-Lee

Daughter of Anne Eatmon and Sterling Gosman (Wikipedia; the UEL blog spells them “Anne Eatman and Stirling Gosman”; the Governor General’s Performing Arts Awards calls her parents “Ann Gosman and the late Reverend Sterling Gosman”).

Portrait via the UEL history blog. No portrait of Anne Eatmon was found in the sources searched.

The University of New Brunswick’s 2011 honorary-degree citation independently confirms the story: as a subject on CBC’s genealogy program, “Measha learned that her ancestors came to Nova Scotia in 1783 among the Black Loyalists fleeing the American revolution. Her four-times-great grandparents settled in Fredericton.” (UNB citation)

Open the LAC record for John Goseman (item 905) →

Routing note: secondary sources say the family first lived in Shelburne and later settled in Fredericton; the LAC entry itself gives the destination as Port Mouton. Port Mouton and Port Roseway (Shelburne) were neighbouring 1783 destinations, so this reads as a routing detail rather than a contradiction — but it is worth knowing.

His daughter — Fanney Gozeman, LAC item 907

Fanney Gozeman (note the spelling), age 1, female, Black, owner Mr Weir, same inspection date, ship, document and page — LAC item 907. Secondary sources call her “five-month-old Fanny,” so there is a small age and spelling discrepancy against the primary record; the identity match (same ship, date, page, owner) is strong.

Not verified: Rose Goseman’s own Book of Negroes entry was not individually located in this research — only John’s (905) and Fanney’s (907) were verified. Secondary sources place Rose with them, but cite no item number for her, so none is given here. No direct CBC page or video for the 2007 Who Do You Think You Are? segment was found either — the UNB citation, Wikipedia, and the UEL blog are the sources describing it.

The Black Loyalist story is now on public display: in April 2026 the Black Loyalist Heritage Centre in Birchtown shared a new informational panel about John Goseman, noting Measha as his descendant, with a photo of her performing — see the Centre’s Instagram post (30 Apr 2026) and Facebook reel (9 Apr 2026).

The key clarification: no source found attributes a Black Loyalist ancestor to the Eatmon (maternal) side. Measha is a Black Loyalist descendant through her father. Her mother Anne Eatmon connects her to Chester Eatmon (§4) and to Elm Hill (§3) — not to a named 1783 entrant.

3 · Elm Hill — why the Eatmons belong to a Black Loyalist community

Elm Hill, in Hampstead Parish, Queens County, New Brunswick, is a historic Black Loyalist settlement. Sources disagree slightly on the founding date — Wikipedia and a June 2026 genealogy post say it was established / founded in 1806 by Black Loyalists from Virginia, while the Provincial Archives of New Brunswick says it was “settled about 1812 by black Loyalists who came from Virginia.” Either way, it is described as one of Canada’s earliest Black communities.

The primary Elm Hill families named in the sources are the McIntyres, Bowleses, Radcliffes — and Eatmons — who “frequently intermarried.” That intermarriage is exactly why the Eatmons are plausibly descendants of the Elm Hill Black Loyalist community by residence and marriage, even though no named Eatmon ancestor has been located in the 1783 Book of Negroes.

  • Elizabeth (Eatmon) Radcliffe — born in Elm Hill, daughter of Simon Eatmon and Phoebe Ann Wright, married Ernest Radcliffe in 1893 — shows the Eatmon presence in Elm Hill through the 1800s, and the Eatmon/Eatman spelling alternation in her census records. (WikiTree)
  • Chester Eatmon himself was born in Elm Hill in 1904, to a McIntyre mother — the intermarriage pattern in his own parentage.

Sources: Wikipedia — Elm Hill, New Brunswick · Instagram genealogy post on Elm Hill families (3 Jun 2026)

4 · Chester Eatmon (1904–1988)

Chester Adolphus Eatmon is the Eatmon at the centre of this story: Elm Hill-born, a Fredericton bricklayer, and a harness-racing fixture who became Canada’s oldest licensed harness driver. He is also Measha Brueggergosman-Lee’s maternal grandfather — her mother Ann (Eatmon) Gosman is Chester’s daughter. That link is confirmed by family obituaries: Edna Jacqueline Murdock’s obituary (she was a daughter of Chester Adolphus Eatmon) lists her surviving sisters as “Ann Gosman and Jellina McGhee” and her brother as “Chester Eatmon II”; Viola Doubledee’s obituary likewise lists “Ann Gosman” among her siblings. He is also your own great-grandfather — your Ancestry tree (§7) runs straight through him.

  • 7 June 1904 — Born in Elm Hill to William Bateman Eatman and Rosella Blanch McIntyre.
  • 10 Nov 1925 — Marries Edna McCarty. He changed his surname from Eatman to Eatmon after marrying.
  • Working life — Bricklayer by trade. He designed and made the “Jesus on the Cross” monument in the Catholic graveyard on Woodstock Road, Fredericton.
  • 1961, age 56/57 — Takes out his harness-racing licence. First horse: Shadow Chief, then Joey’s Spirit.
  • By age 79 — About 800 races. A fixture at Fredericton Raceway for 26 years.
  • Age 82 — Canada’s oldest licensed harness racing driver.
  • Family — Fathered 21 children with his first wife Edna, and raised 11 children with his second wife.
  • July 1988 — Dies in Fredericton. Date discrepancy: MyNewBrunswick gives 21 July 1988; WikiTree gives 25 July 1988. Buried in Sunny Bank Cemetery, Devon, beside Edna.

Biography sources: New Brunswick Black History Society — Chester Eatmon · MyNewBrunswick — Chester Eatmon (photo source for the gallery below) · Obituaries: Edna Jacqueline Murdock, Viola Doubledee.

Chester in print — the Windsor Star, 8 August 1986

Your Ancestry tree’s gallery for Chester holds a Newspapers.com clipping that is a genuine newspaper story about him in his lifetime: The Windsor Star, 8 August 1986, p. 16 — “Chester’s still sulky-ing around” (also syndicated in The Record, Hackensack, NJ, 11 August 1986, p. 42). It reports Chester, father of 21 children, as at 82 Canada’s oldest licensed harness-racing driver — the article says probably the oldest active harness-racing driver in North America. He started training and driving trotters at 65 after retiring, and had been a fixture at Fredericton Raceway for 20 years. His favourite horse was Joey Spirit, given to him free as a six-year-old, retired at 14, “always in the money” — and later stolen off the property. The photo caption reads: “GIVE UP RACING? No way, says 82-year-old Chester Eatmon” (Photo/Canadian Press). In his own words:

“I don’t race for the money — although it’s nice when it comes along — I race for the glory and the thrill.” — Chester Eatmon, The Windsor Star, 8 August 1986

One flag: the article names his wife “Bessie.” Edna died on 18 December 1981, so this may be a second marriage — it is unverified, and no source consulted confirms it. (It also sits beside the §4 note that he “raised 11 children with his second wife” — the two are not tied together here as fact.)

Source: Newspapers.com clipping held in Chester Adolphus Eatmon’s gallery in your Ancestry tree (§7), read in the second Ancestry dig, 11 November 2026. Chester’s gallery also holds items titled “Birth Certificate Chester Eatman,” “EATMON, CHESTER ADOLPHUS,” “Chester Eatman – birth,” and an “Android Photo” (a group photo of four people with a horse — his profile image).

Photos of Chester — tap any photo to enlarge

Chester Eatmon Jr.

Chester’s son, Chester Eatmon II, was also a horseman: he received the Pioneer Award at the Fredericton Horsemen’s Association banquet in April 2014 (Standardbred Canada). A January 2026 Fredericton Raceway “Golden Jubilee” drivers list gives career figures for both men — Jr.: $34,461 / 50 wins; Sr.: $5,911 / 17 wins (The Fredericton Scene).

5 · “Chester is in the news” — what was actually found

You mentioned Chester Eatmon is in the news. The research looked hard for that story, and here is the honest result: Chester Eatmon Sr. died in 1988, and no current mainstream news story about him was found. A site search of CBC for “Eatmon” returned nothing, and no 2025–26 mainstream article about Chester Sr. turned up. If you have a specific story in mind, its outlet or date would be needed to pin it down — it was not locatable by name search.

Recent mentions of Chester (tributes and exhibits, not news stories)

One real newspaper story about Chester from his lifetime was found — not in current news, but in your Ancestry tree’s gallery: The Windsor Star, 8 August 1986, “Chester’s still sulky-ing around.” It is told in full in §4.

  • 5 Sep 2025 — A Facebook tribute by his granddaughter Nyja Jessie, with a colourised photo of Chester with a horse and a UNB poster, and warm comments from people who knew him.
  • Jan–Feb 2024 — The UNB Art Centre’s Rediscovering the Roots of Black New Brunswickers exhibition added nine new portrait panels, including one for Chester Eatmon. (UNB, Jan 2024 · UNB Art Centre exhibition page)
  • Jan 2026 — The Fredericton Scene blog’s “Golden Jubilee” drivers list names Chester Sr. and Jr. (linked in §4).
  • 2006 — A newspaper race result, “Pair shine at EPR,” lists “R G Indy (Chester Eatmon) in 2:05 4-5” (via the MBRL/Postmedia catalogue).

⚠ The Eatmon actually in Fredericton news in 2025–26 is a different man — Christopher Isaiah Eatmon, not Chester.

The Fredericton Independent reported on 15 July 2026 (“The evidentiary gaps are numerous,” by Don MacPherson) that Judge Scott Brittain acquitted Christopher Isaiah Eatmon, 32, of Fredericton, of fentanyl, weapons and stolen-property charges (decision 26 June 2026), citing shortcomings in surveillance. Earlier coverage in the same outlet: “Fentanyl-production suspect denies charges” (11 Sep 2025) and “Drug defendant won’t challenge warrant” (22 Dec 2025). Do not conflate him with Chester.

Two other look-alikes to keep separate: Cortez Eatmon, 25, shot and killed by police in Kennesaw, Georgia, on 27 May 2026 — a different person in a different country; and a Chester Eatmon, 19, in Pontiac, Michigan, in a 1967 attempted-burglary report (Pontiac Press, 29 May 1967) — also a different person. Neither belongs to the Fredericton family story.

One more dead end, checked for completeness: the town of Chester, Nova Scotia, has no Eatmon link in the records searched. It was a Planter/Loyalist town; Black Loyalist Samuel Ball moved there from Shelburne (children born there 1798–1805), but no record connects an Eatmon to Chester, NS.

6 · They served — the Eatmans’ military service

Researched for Remembrance Day, 11 November 2026. The family produced at least seven verified service members across the two world wars — one of them killed in action. Military records spell the name Eatman throughout. Each entry below carries its source, and anything resting on a single source — or on secondary sources only — is flagged as such rather than stated as settled fact.

Sgt Arthur Wallace “Duke” Eatman (1920–1943) — killed in action, Sicily

The family’s only war death found in the Canadian Virtual War Memorial. Arthur Eatman led a 28-man reconnaissance patrol in Sicily during Operation Husky and did not come back.

Rank / unit
Sergeant, Carleton and York Regiment, R.C.I.C.
Service number
G/18010
Born
15 May 1920, Fredericton, NB — son of James W. and Thursa L. Eatman, of Barker’s Point, York Co., NB
Enlisted
September 1939, Woodstock, NB — date disputed: the Canadian Virtual War Memorial gives 7 September 1939; the New Brunswick Museum gives 3 September 1939. The follow-up research found the weight of evidence favours 3 September — a 2019 UNB study working directly from Arthur’s service file gives 3 September — but the conflict is not resolved. The idea that 3 September was enrolment and 7 September the attestation/recorded date is a hypothesis only; it was not proven from the file.
Promotions
Lance-Corporal April 1940; Acting Corporal, confirmed September 1940; Acting Lance-Sergeant with pay August 1941, confirmed Lance-Sergeant November 1941; attended CMHQ Course 801 (Battle Drill), 4–26 July 1942, as Acting Sergeant; promoted Sergeant about October 1942 (UNB study, from his service file)
Overseas
Sailed on SS Monarch of Bermuda 9 December 1939, departing Halifax 10 December; landed in Sicily about noon on 10 July 1943 (UNB study)
Died
22 July 1943, age 23 (official date, Veterans Affairs Canada / Commonwealth War Graves Commission)
The patrol
Twenty-eight men of “A” Company under Eatman were sent to check whether a nearby house was occupied by enemy forces. The patrol did not return. Five bodies were recovered — Eatman, Acting Lance-Corporal W. J. Lapointe, and Privates Omar Gallagher, W. J. McCauley and W. H. Morris; twenty-two men were later revealed as prisoners of war; Pte Arlie Hanson was never recovered and is presumed killed in action. (New Brunswick Museum, 2 Feb 2026; UNB study)
Where it happened
No exact spot is established. The regiment held a patrol base in the Dittaino River valley near the Raddusa–Agira train station from 21 July 1943, and Duke’s body was recovered the next day by “C” Company about 2,000 yards forward of the regiment’s position. The patrol’s exact location is disputed: the commanding officer, Lt-Col Dodd Tweedie, said a house within eyesight of the position; Brigade Major Pangman said the area around Mount Scalpello, about 7 miles east. Even the timing is disputed — the regimental war diary says the patrol went out on the night of 23 July, while other accounts, including survivor Cpl Marshall Boone’s diary, say mid-morning. (UNB study, from the Carleton and York Regiment war diary, July 1943 — RG 24-C-3, Vol. 15050, file 43)
Service file
Library and Archives Canada, Service Files of the Second World War – War Dead, 1939–1947: RG 24, Volume 25803, Item 10283 (cited in the UNB study’s bibliography). The file itself was not opened in this research — LAC’s search was blocked partway through the follow-up pass — so nothing below is claimed from reading it directly.
Buried
Agira Canadian War Cemetery, Sicily — grave reference C, C, 288. Agira is confirmed as his burial place; sources do not settle it as the exact place of death.
Commemorated
Page 156 of the Second World War Book of Remembrance; his name, “Arthur W. Eatman,” is inscribed on the Carleton and York Regiment Memorial in Fredericton (dedicated 8 May 1998)
Awards
No gallantry award recorded — the Commonwealth War Graves Commission entry’s Honours field is blank (no gallantry award or Mention in Despatches). Campaign-medal entitlement is unverified: no source read documents it. The place to check is the Ancestry “genealogy package” for his LAC file (RG 24, Vol. 25803, Item 10283), which would contain the medal entitlement form — it was not examined in this research. LAC’s own guidance also notes that war-dead files “do not indicate the locations of overseas postings or list battles in which an individual may have participated.”

The UNB Art Centre’s Black History Month project — which gives him his nickname, “Duke” — calls him “amongst the only visible examples of a Black non-commissioned officer serving in a non-segregated unit,” and notes he attended Charlotte Street School, Fredericton, and went overseas with the 1st Canadian Division in December 1939. A 2012 York-Sunbury Historical Society talk by Dr. Lee Windsor was titled “A Black Leader of White Men: Sergeant Arthur Eatman with the Carleton and York Regiment at War in Sicily, 1943.” His Second World War service file survives in Library and Archives Canada’s “WWII Records and Service Files of War Dead, 1939–1947” — the exact reference, RG 24, Volume 25803, Item 10283, is now known from the UNB study’s bibliography — but the file itself was not opened in this research. One caution on his birth date: the UNB study is internally inconsistent, giving 15 May 1920 in its introduction and Chapter 3 but 20 May 1920 in a Chapter 2 footnote; Veterans Affairs Canada, the War Graves Commission and the New Brunswick Museum all say 15 May 1920, which is the date used here.

Arthur in photographs and memorials — the follow-up finds

  • The 1939 Woodstock training photos (Belyea fonds). The New Brunswick Museum’s February 2026 article reproduces four photographs from fall 1939 at the Carleton and York Regimental Depot, Woodstock, NB (Nov/Dec 1939, silver prints, photographer unknown; image files BelyeaAB-F34-1, -3, -4, -5), from militaria the Museum acquired from Abner Barnett Belyea (1893–1990), a First World War veteran; the photos were sent by his half-brother Russell Vernon Belyea (1920–2003), who enlisted with the regiment. Captions name Eatman alongside Belyea, Sergeant Savage, Close, Seeley, Rosario Blaquiere, Doncaster, Crouse, Chase and Green. (New Brunswick Museum)
  • NBM Facebook video, 2 February 2026. A short Black History Month video reuses further photographs: three Second World War soldiers outside a wooden barracks, Eatman identified as the central figure; a group of about 11 soldiers with rifles in front of the same building; “Carleton and York Regiment No. 1 Section, Platoon 1,” including Eatman; and a final image captioned “Training at the Regimental Depot Woodstock, New Brunswick.” Commenters mention visits to Agira Canadian War Cemetery and share family photographs of Carleton and York relatives. (New Brunswick Museum on Facebook)
  • Royal New Brunswick Regiment tribute, 16 December 2024. A three-image carousel: a portrait of Sgt Eatman, his War Graves headstone, and a wooden plaque with a mounted rifle engraved in memory of Sgt Eatman, held by two Canadian Armed Forces members and a civilian. (Royal New Brunswick Regiment on Facebook)
  • Carleton and York Regiment Memorial, Fredericton. Veterans Affairs Canada’s memorial inventory: Memorial Number 13004-017, Carleton Street, Fredericton Armoury (GPS 45.963175, −66.640257); dedicated 8 May 1998; erected by the Carleton and York Regiment Association. (Veterans Affairs Canada — National Inventory of Canadian Military Memorials)
  • Fredericton Cenotaph. Dedicated 11 November 1923; bronze plaques were later added commemorating those who fell in the Second World War and the Korean War (Memorial 13004-016). Whether Arthur Eatman’s name appears on the Second World War plaque is not confirmed. (Veterans Affairs Canada — memorial inventory)
  • His Virtual War Memorial gallery holds images captioned “Fredericton War Memorial,” “Agira Canadian War Cemetery,” “View of Mt. Enna,” and “Memorial.” The regiment’s history, Robert Tooley’s Invicta: The Carleton and York Regiment in the Second World War (1989), notes “at least four blacks” in the regiment, including Duke and First World War veteran Seymour Tyler, plus Indigenous soldiers. (Canadian Virtual War Memorial — Arthur Wallace Eatman)

Sources: Canadian Virtual War Memorial — Arthur Wallace Eatman · New Brunswick Museum — “A Snapshot in Time” (2 Feb 2026) · UNB Art Centre — Black History Month · Veterans Affairs Canada — Carleton and York Regiment Memorial · UNB Scholar — “Making it up as you go: racial policy in the Canadian military during the two world wars” (a study built on James’s and Arthur’s personnel files)

Eldridge “Gus” Eatman (1880–1960) — the sprinter who had to join the British Army

Before he was a soldier, Gus Eatman was one of Canada’s great sprinters (see §8). When war broke out he was in New Brunswick — and, in the Canadian Encyclopedia’s words, “the Canadian Army was not accepting Black Canadian recruits, so he went to England.” In 1915 he enlisted in the British Army, serving with the Northumberland Fusiliers (also given as the 2nd Battalion, Royal Northumberland Fusiliers). A photograph of him in uniform doing rifle drill appeared on the front page of the British Daily Mirror on 6 March 1915. He arrived in France on 8 June 1915, was promoted to corporal, and was wounded in the leg at the Battle of Loos. His battalion transferred to Salonika in late October 1915 and stayed until June 1918; he was discharged on 26 June 1918.

Handle with care: Eatman’s British service record was destroyed in a fire during the London Blitz in the Second World War. Everything above therefore rests on secondary sources — the Canadian Encyclopedia, CommunityStories, the NB Black History Society, the NB Sports Hall of Fame and Athletics Canada — not on an archival file. The NB Black History Society’s figure of 785 days in frontline trenches is one such secondary-source claim and is not presented here as archival fact. His 1935 campaign to raise an Ethiopian Foreign Legion against Mussolini’s invasion was activism, not military service, and is not counted as such.

Sources: The Canadian Encyclopedia — Eldridge Eatman · CommunityStories — “Our Black Heritage” · NB Black History Society · Athletics Canada (14 Mar 2023)

John Wesley Eatman & Manzer Eatman — No. 2 Construction Battalion, “the Black Battalion”

Pte John Wesley Eatman
Regimental no. 931125 · born 18 April 1898, Fredericton, NB · enlisted at Pictou, NS, 14 August 1916 · next of kin: his father, William Bateman Eatman, Fredericton, NB · LAC: RG 150, Accession 1992-93/166, Box 2812-14. His occupation and physical description were not obtained — his attestation image was not read (see the access note below)
Pte Manzer Eatman
Regimental no. 931124 · born 6 April 1882 · enlisted at Pictou, NS, 14 August 1916 · LAC: RG 150, Accession 1992-93/166, Box 2812-17 (Item ID 371828) — his date of birth and box number, both missing before, were established in the follow-up pass from his attestation paper, read in full at Library and Archives Canada
Both
On the battalion’s nominal roll of 28 March 1917, departing Halifax aboard SS Southland

No. 2 Construction Battalion, CEF — created 5 July 1916 — was a segregated, non-combatant unit: “the first and only all-Black battalion-sized formation in Canadian military history.” It arrived in Liverpool on 7 April 1917, was reorganised as a labour company, and served in the Jura region of eastern France from 17 May 1917 with the Canadian Forestry Corps — cutting timber, building and maintaining roads, railways and camp services. It was disbanded in September 1920. Canada issued a National Apology to the battalion’s descendants on 9 July 2022, and the battle honour “France and Flanders, 1917–18” was awarded on 1 June 2022; the battalion is perpetuated by 4 Engineer Support Regiment, CFB Gagetown, NB.

Manzer’s attestation paper — read in full (LAC, follow-up pass)

Next of kin — conflict
The two records disagree, and neither is presented here as settled. His attestation paper names a next of kin whose name reads “Eldridge Eatman” (handwriting uncertain; the entry appears corrected/overwritten), at an address ending “Washington D.C.,” with the relationship stated as “wife.” The Nova Scotia Archives nominal roll instead lists his next of kin as “Eatman, William, Washington, D.C., U.S.A.” A re-read of the image would be needed to settle it.

Source: Library and Archives Canada — Manzer Eatman personnel record (Item ID 371828), read live in the follow-up pass; nominal roll: Nova Scotia Archives — No. 2 Construction Battalion nominal roll. Manzer’s box (2812-17) sits right beside James Wallace Eatman’s (2812-13) and John Wesley Eatman’s (2812-14), consistent with alphabetical filing. An access note on this research: after the first successful LAC search (Manzer), LAC’s bot protection blocked every further live search in the follow-up session, so the remaining men’s LAC details come from search-indexed LAC pages and Fold3, which republishes LAC data — not from live LAC reads.

The Fredericton Region Museum lists “John Wesley Eatman, son of William B. Eatman of Zealand” and “Manzer Eatman, brother of Eldridge and William B Eatman of Zealand” among the York and Sunbury County men who went overseas with the battalion in March 1917. One caution: a CommunityStories page calls John Eldridge’s cousin — but if William B. was Eldridge’s brother, John would be his nephew. The exact relationship is not asserted here without a family-tree source.

The battalion’s story is on tour now: the Fredericton Region Museum’s travelling exhibition Forgotten Loyalty: New Brunswick’s Hidden Connection to the No. 2 Construction Battalion, curated by Jennifer Dow, runs at Government House to 19 April 2026, then the Canadian Military Engineers Museum (CFB Gagetown) 1 Jul 2026 – 17 Jan 2027, the NB Black History Museum 1 Feb – 1 May 2027, the Fredericton Region Museum 1 Jun – 8 Aug 2027, and the NB Military History Museum 1 Sep 2027 – 1 Apr 2028, with a virtual exhibition due in 2027.

Sources: Nova Scotia Archives — No. 2 Construction Battalion Nominal Roll · Library and Archives Canada — John W. Eatman, personnel records · Canada.ca — No. 2 Construction Battalion · Canada.ca — National Apology Advisory Committee report · Fredericton Region Museum — “Honouring the No. 2 Construction Battalion” (2022) · Fredericton Region Museum — Forgotten Loyalty exhibition

Joseph Eatmon & Mansfield Eatmon — two more names in the CEF index

Ancestry’s “Canada, World War I CEF Attestation Papers, 1914–1918” index holds exactly five Eatman/Eatmon records — James Wallace, Joseph, Manzer, Mansfield and John Wesley. The follow-up pass established what it could for the two men this page had not covered before:

Joseph Eatmon
Regimental no. 2246174 · born 19 February 1898, Fredericton, NB · residence Fredericton, NB · next of kin: his mother, Lily McIntyre · served for Canada in the First World War (Fold3 index, derived from LAC records). His unit, LAC box number, enlistment date and place, occupation and physical description were not obtained — his attestation image was not read. The high regimental number is consistent with a late-war / 1918 enlistment, but that is inference, not a record fact.
Mansfield Eatmon
Born 22 January 1888, Elm Hill — and that is all that is established. His regimental number, unit, LAC box number, enlistment date and place, occupation and physical description were not found in any record consulted. His attestation paper exists (Ancestry indexes it; LAC holds the file) but was not read: LAC’s search was blocked during the follow-up pass and Ancestry’s live search requires an account. The only lead is his next of kin — see the Hannah note below. Note he is a different person from Dubert Mansfield Eatman (b. ~1908, below).

Sources: Fold3 — Joseph Eatmon, “Canada, Soldiers of the First World War, 1914–1918” · Fold3 — John W. Eatman · Ancestry — CEF Attestation Papers index, surname Eatman (search-result snippets; personal-data fields masked, live search requires an account)

“Mrs Hannah Eatmon” — next of kin, not a servicewoman. She appears in the CEF attestation index, and the follow-up established by elimination that she was a next of kin listed on someone else’s papers, not a soldier in her own right: Ancestry’s CEF attestation index contains exactly five Eatman/Eatmon records, all men — there is no attestation paper for a Hannah Eatmon as a recruit. Hannah (Holmes) Eatman was the wife of Major Eatman and the mother of James Wallace Eatman (§6, above).

Most likely she is Mansfield Eatmon’s next of kin — probable, not proven. In that index, Mansfield’s Next of Kin field is a masked three-token value ending in “Eatmon” whose character pattern matches “Mrs Hannah Eatmon,” and the other men’s next of kin are accounted for differently — Joseph’s is his mother Lily McIntyre, Manzer’s is his wife, John’s is his father William Bateman. James’s paper was not re-checked in the follow-up pass, so he cannot be fully eliminated — though as a man married to Thursa since 1904, his next of kin would ordinarily have been his wife. Whether Mansfield was a son of Major and Hannah is likewise not established — a plausible hypothesis (same Elm Hill family, same “Eatmon” spelling, born 1888), not a record fact, and it is not stated as one here. Sources: Genealogy.com forum — Thomas Murray, 3 Dec 2008 (Hannah as Major’s wife and James’s mother), corroborated by the UNB study; Ancestry CEF index as above.

Two more brothers — one now corroborated, one still single-source

Dubert — now corroborated by a second source. The New Brunswick Museum’s 2026 article states that Arthur’s brother Pte Dubert Mansfield Eatman served with Canadian Forestry Corps No. 4. The follow-up pass found a second source: the 2019 UNB study states “Dubert, his eldest brother, served with the Canadian Forestry Corps for the duration of the war” (Chapter 3 — the sentence itself is uncited, but the chapter is built from Arthur’s file and related records). No obituary or separate service record for Dubert was found. Dubert Mansfield Eatman (b. ~1908, son of James) is a different person from Mansfield Eatmon (b. 1888, Elm Hill, above).

Harry Ellis — still single-source. Pte Harry Ellis Eatman, U.S. Army, 304th Bombardment Group, Army Air Forces, rests on the Museum article alone; no U.S. enlistment record for him was found. One unproven lead from the UNB study: Arthur’s file records that as of October 1942 his brother Henry “was recorded as missing by the U.S. Government from Virginia Air Base,” and the 304th Bombardment Group was associated with Langley Field, Virginia. Henry and Harry may be the same man — not proven; treat it as a lead only. For the family frame: James’s children as listed in June 1916 paperwork (UNB study) were Thelma Leon (12), Dubert Mansfield (8), Henry (6), Mabel (4) and Blanche (1), with Arthur Wallace the seventh child; an eighth sibling, Hilda Rosebud, is listed as deceased as of 14 January 1942 in Arthur’s file.

Who did not serve — and the searches that came up empty

  • Chester Eatmon (1904–1988) — no military service found. The harness racer of §4 is not a veteran in any source found; UNB lists him as “Harness racer,” not a soldier. Do not confuse him with a different Chester Eatmon (b. 21 December 1947, U.S. Army, Vietnam era, d. 21 October 1973) in the U.S. VA BIRLS death file.
  • Korea and later — checked in the follow-up pass, with limits stated plainly: no Canadian Eatmon/Eatman in Korea was found. The only Eatmons the Korea searches returned were unrelated Americans — John D. Eatmon (Jacksonville, FL, U.S. Army veteran of Korea, d. 26 Aug 2006); James Thurmon Eatmon (U.S. Air Force, WWII/Korea/Vietnam, 1917–2005); Norwood Talmage Eatmon (U.S. Navy, Korea, 1933–2016); and James P. Eatmon (11th Airborne Division, Ft. Campbell, KY, during the Korean War, 1931–2022) — none connected to the New Brunswick family. The Korean War Book of Remembrance holds 516 names and no Eatman/Eatmon was found among them in web searches — but this was not verified by a working Virtual War Memorial surname search: when tested on 11 November 2026, the CVWM surname search did not execute as a filter (it returned the default listing, not surname-filtered results), so it is not cited here as a completed check. And there is a structural limit: LAC’s post-1945 service files, Korea included, are restricted and available only by ATIP request — there is no public searchable database, so absence of a public record cannot by itself prove no service. (Library and Archives Canada — ATIP guidance)
  • The Elm Hill in-law families: no service record was found for Marshall Bowles, Ernest Radcliffe, or James Henry Bowles (1888–1957) — even though the McIntyre, Bowles, Radcliffe and Eatmon families of Elm Hill frequently intermarried. One McIntyre does appear on the No. 2 nominal roll — Pte Charles Theodore McIntyre (931102), of Saint John, enlisted 10 August 1916 — but no source connects him to the Elm Hill McIntyres or to Rosella Blanch McIntyre, Chester’s mother. He is not claimed as family here.
  • Maurice Eatman — Eldridge’s third cousin, who campaigned for his Sports Hall of Fame induction — has no military service found.

From the same community — context, not kin

These Black soldiers came from the same Fredericton / York–Sunbury community. They are context for a Remembrance Day read — not Eatman relatives, and no source consulted claims otherwise:

  • Bugle Sergeant Arthur “Seymour” Tyler (1897–1985) — enlisted in No. 2 Construction Battalion 14 September 1916; later a Second World War Bugle Sergeant with the Carleton and York Regiment; his leg was broken in seven places in bombing during the Battle of Britain (1941) and he returned to Canada that year. Caution: a story repeated by the NB Black History Society that he served with the 8th Battalion (90th Rifles) is explicitly called false by the Black Canadian Veterans site — he was never a member of that battalion. (Black Canadian Veterans · CommunityStories)
  • Sapper Miles Smith Dymond (b. 1882, Fredericton) — 1st (Brighton) Field Company, Canadian Engineers; enlisted at Valcartier 23 September 1914; in France 18 March 1915; fought at 2nd Ypres, the Somme, Vimy Ridge, Hill 70 and Passchendaele; buried by shell fire on at least three occasions; discharged December 1918. Dymond is also Eldridge Eatman’s mother’s maiden name (Jane Diamond/Dymond) — but no source consulted proves Miles’s exact kinship to Eldridge, so none is claimed. (Roberts Publications · Veterans Affairs Canada — Black Canadians in uniform)
  • Pte Robert Henry, Pte Cyril Henry and Cpl Arthur William McCarthy — Black Carleton and York Regiment soldiers in the Second World War, described as brothers-in-arms of Arthur Eatman. Not Eatman kin. (CommunityStories)

What Ancestry adds — and what it doesn’t (yet)

The one confirmed Ancestry finding: Ancestry’s Canadian Expeditionary Force attestation index lists Manzer as “Manzer Eatmon [Manzer Eatman]” — the clearest single proof that the Eatmon and Eatman spellings are the same man and the same family. It is also a practical search tip: on Ancestry, as everywhere else, search Eatman, Eatmon, and Eastman.

What the Ancestry record search adds: searching Ancestry’s Canadian records for “Eatmon” returns 8 results, all Canadian Expeditionary Force, 1914–1918 — including Joseph Eatmon and Mansfield Eatmon (both covered above), alongside Manzer Eatmon’s personnel file. Searching “Eatman” returns 11 results, including the attestation papers of James Wallace and John Wesley Eatman and Arthur Wallace Eatman’s Second World War war-dead file. Joseph and Mansfield Eatmon are not in your own tree (§7). No military record or hint is attached to Chester, William B, John, or Simon Lomax Eatmon in your tree — the military material belongs to collateral Eatmon/Eatman men found by record search.

What the follow-up pass settled since: Manzer’s birth date (6 April 1882) and LAC box (2812-17) were established from his attestation paper read at LAC — his Ancestry-indexed details had been masked in the search results consulted earlier. James Wallace Eatman’s LAC box (2812-13) and Arthur’s exact war-dead file reference (RG 24, Vol. 25803, Item 10283) are likewise now known. “Mrs Hannah Eatmon” is a next of kin, most likely Mansfield’s — not a servicewoman (see above).

The signed-in follow-ups that would still move the hunt: (1) Arthur’s war-dead file itself — via the Ancestry “genealogy package” for RG 24, Vol. 25803, Item 10283 — for the medal entitlement form and anything that settles the 3 vs 7 September 1939 enlistment date; (2) Mansfield Eatmon’s attestation paper (indexed by Ancestry, held by LAC) for his regimental number, unit and description, and to confirm the “Mrs Hannah Eatmon” next-of-kin reading; (3) Joseph Eatmon’s attestation paper for his unit and enlistment details; (4) Harry Ellis Eatman in the U.S. National Archives to lift him from single-source to confirmed.

Military open questions — updated by the follow-up pass

  • Arthur’s enlistment date — narrowed, not resolved: 3 September 1939 (New Brunswick Museum, and the UNB study working from his service file) vs 7 September 1939 (Canadian Virtual War Memorial). The enrolment-vs-attestation explanation is a hypothesis only. His file (RG 24, Vol. 25803, Item 10283) was identified but not opened.
  • Arthur’s campaign medals: no gallantry award is recorded (War Graves Honours field blank); campaign-medal entitlement is unverified — the medal form in his Ancestry genealogy package was not examined.
  • Where Arthur died: no exact spot is established — the Dittaino River valley near the Raddusa–Agira station is the closest detail, with the precise location (and even the patrol’s timing) disputed between accounts. Agira is confirmed as the burial place only.
  • Mansfield Eatmon: regimental number, unit, LAC box, enlistment details, occupation and description all still unknown — his attestation paper exists but was not read (LAC blocked; Ancestry account-gated).
  • Joseph Eatmon: unit, LAC box, enlistment date/place, occupation and description still unknown.
  • John Wesley Eatman: occupation and physical description still unknown — his attestation image was not read.
  • Manzer Eatman: birth date and LAC box are now known (above); what remains open is the next-of-kin conflict — his attestation paper’s uncertain, apparently corrected “wife” entry vs the nominal roll’s William Eatman of Washington, D.C. — and the uncertain “Farmer” reading of his trade.
  • Harry Ellis Eatman: still single-source; the “Henry missing from Virginia Air Base” lead is unproven.
  • Korea: no Canadian Eatmon/Eatman found — but the Virtual War Memorial surname search did not function as a filter when tested, and post-1945 files are ATIP-only, so Korea service can be neither confirmed nor ruled out from public records alone.
  • Fredericton Cenotaph: whether Arthur Eatman’s name is on the Second World War plaque is unconfirmed.
  • “Mrs Hannah Eatmon”: her identification as Mansfield Eatmon’s next of kin is probable, not proven (masked index value; James’s paper not re-checked), and whether Mansfield was Major and Hannah’s son is unproven.
  • Eldridge Eatman: British file destroyed in the Blitz — battalion details, the Loos/Salonika timeline and the 785-days figure remain secondary-source only. The Daily Mirror front-page photograph of 6 March 1915 is a contemporary corroboration, but was not itself viewed in this research.

What is free on the compare pages: Otis — 58 shared DNA matches, an ethnicity comparison, the shared journey “Northern New England Settlers,” “Common ancestors in trees: None of the ancestors in your tree are also in Otis Eatmon’s tree,” and “Matching surnames in trees: 1 surname” (the surname itself is unreadable — clicking redirects to Join). An Eatmon-surname search of your DNA matches returned 18 matches, including Elijah Nathan Troy Chamberlain (1,057 cM, 1st cousin, maternal), cory pennicott (801 cM, half uncle), Mona Roy (261 cM — the Find a Grave contributor above), Wyatt Paige (252 cM), H. Gabriel Gibson (192 cM) and Jemika Davidson (169 cM). DANIEL — 124 shared DNA matches; the compare page says “Common ancestors found” but viewing them requires membership; “Matching surnames in trees: None of the last names in your tree are also in DANIEL Gosman’s tree.” A Gosman-surname search returned 3 matches: DANIEL Gosman (48 cM), Alyson Claybourne (33 cM, public tree, 13 people) and crystal powell (24 cM, public tree, 143 people, common ancestor).

Also locked among the 51 Eatmon-filtered hints: Major’s Newspapers.com obituary index, the NB Marriages record for “Majer Eatmon” and Hannah Holmes, the 1861/1871/1881/1891/1901 censuses, a Newspapers.com story “Mrs. Eatman” (1 Dec 1882, Saint John); Clark’s Newspapers.com story (29 Jun 1965) and voters lists; William B’s marriage index, NB Deaths, NB Marriages and Drouin records; a Newspapers.com story for Lisa Rose Eatmon (7 Aug 1987); Edna’s obituary collection, marriage index, voters lists and baptism; Lomax’s NB Marriages record — “Simon Eatmon” m. “Pheobe Eatmon,” a possible first or other wife, distinct from Caroline; and Chester’s obituary index and voters lists. McCarty-side photo hints (also locked, descriptions visible) include Charles King McCarty’s “Early Negro Cemetery Prior to the Dam” — a map of Kingsclear Cemetery before the Mactaquac Dam — and a “Cemetery Relocation Project Doc” stating the “Early Negro Cemetery” is listed as “not to be moved or disturbed,” and that Charles King McCarty remained in the ground when it was flooded by the Mactaquac Dam.

Tree data-quality flags — read before trusting the tree

  • “James Eatmen” is a duplicate, not a separate ancestor. The tree entry “James Eatmen” (b. 1828, listed as a 3rd great-grandmother) is a second entry for the same woman as Tamar Hopewell: same parents — Richard Hopewell (1792–1888) and Sara Patterson (1791–1866) — and the same sons, William B Eatmon (b. 1847, Kingsclear) and Major Eatmon (b. Jan 1855, Elm Hill). Also listed: half-siblings Caroline Hopewell (1818–1888) and John Pompey Ramsey Hopewell (1823–1890, listed twice); Sara Patterson d. 1866, Elm Hill; Richard Hopewell d. 11 May 1888, NB. Treat “James Eatmen” as a mis-entered duplicate to reconcile.
  • Rosella McIntyre’s death year conflicts: 1946 (two photo hints) vs abt 1964 (one photo hint).
  • Ella M. Eatmon — daughter or daughter-in-law? The 1911 census index lists Ella M. as Major’s daughter (28); Major’s Find a Grave bio lists her as daughter-in-law. The two disagree. They also disagree on the infant grandson: Lonson M., 4 months, per the census, vs an unnamed “?” per the bio.
  • William McIntyre’s birth year conflicts: 1841 (as Rosella’s “Potential” father, with Deborah A. Cameron 1840–1935) vs 1835 (free-hints listing: b. 1835 Hampstead, d. 10 Dec 1899 Hampstead); his child Charlotte Eatman is also listed. (And note the marriage certificate above names Rosella’s father simply as William McIntyre.)
  • William B’s parents conflict (from the marriage-certificate flag above): “John & Betsy Eatman” on the certificate vs mother Tamar Hopewell (1828–1916) on Find a Grave — unresolved.
  • Spelling drift: the tree spells the surname inconsistently — Eatmon / Eatman / Eatmen — while records use “Eatman” most often (“Major Thomas Eatman” appears on the photo hints).

Elm Hill and Fredericton in your own tree

  • Elm Hill, Queens County: birthplace in hints of John Debois Eatmon (1825, hint only); death place in hints of Simon Lomax Eatmon; birthplace in the tree of Alberta Maxime Eatmon (b. 13 Apr 1929); a member photo, “Farm picture of Elm Hill,” is attached to Major Eatmon — your 2nd great-granduncle, a son of John Debois Eatmon.
  • Fredericton: Chester died and is buried there (1988), as is Clark Nicholas Eatmon; Arthur Wallace Eatman was born there in 1920 (see §6).
  • Gagetown, Queens County: Chester was born there (1904) and married there (1925). Kingsclear, York County: William B Eatmon was born there (1847). Burials for John, Lomax, and Major appear in Find a Grave hints for Hampstead, Queens County.

A possible close link — hint-level sources only, not verified. A Find a Grave hint names “Private James Wallace Eatman” (§6) as a child of Major Eatmon, and Major’s Find a Grave memorial bio (above) likewise lists “Pvt James Wallace Eatman 1882–1956” among Major’s children. Major is your 2nd great-granduncle. If that is right, Sgt Arthur Wallace “Duke” Eatman would be your 2nd cousin twice removed. Both sources are hint/contributor level, not primary records, so it is not stated as fact anywhere on this page.

And the Black Loyalist question, on Ancestry: nothing in your account states that any Eatmon, Eatman, or Gosman ancestor was a Black Loyalist — no record or hint reviewed uses the term or names a Loyalist-era origin. Your tree’s earliest Eatmon, Simon Lomax Eatmon, was born in 1800, a generation after 1783. That is a gap in the evidence, not a finding either way.

Limits of these reads: many hint details and record images are membership-locked (see the locked box above — all 63 member photos, all 10 stories, all 77 member trees, and the Otis Eatmon / DANIEL Gosman tree previews were not read, and nothing about them is guessed), and the account names no shared ancestor for either key DNA match. Living people are named only as they appear in your own tree.

8 · Other notable Eatmans & Eatmons

No other Eatmon/Eatman was found in the Book of Negroes, Birchtown, Shelburne, Halifax, Preston, or Sierra Leone records searched. What the record does hold is a remarkable 19th–20th-century Black New Brunswick family:

Eldridge “Gus” Eatman

12 Mar 1880, Zealand Station, NB – 15 Aug 1960, Saint John

Son of John L. and Jane (née Diamond) Eatman. Black Canadian sprinter — Powderhall Trophy winner in 1906, Canadian 100-yard record of 9.8 seconds in 1905, WWI veteran, and inducted into the Saint John, New Brunswick, and Maritime Sports Halls of Fame.

Wikipedia · Athletics Canada, 14 Mar 2023

Sgt Arthur Wallace “Duke” Eatman

15 May 1920, Fredericton – 22 Jul 1943, Sicily

Son of James Wallace Eatman (1882–1956, WWI veteran) and Thursa Levina Wright. Served with the Carleton and York Regiment; killed leading a patrol in Sicily and buried in Agira Canadian War Cemetery. Full service record in §6.

New Brunswick Museum · Veterans Affairs Canada

The No. 2 Construction Battalion Eatmans

First World War

John Wesley Eatman (son of William B. Eatman of Zealand) and Manzer Eatman (brother of Eldridge and William B. Eatman) both served in Canada’s segregated Black battalion.

Fredericton Region Museum

Jocelyn Eatmon Stevens

Social advocate

Listed by the UNB Art Centre among the Black New Brunswickers honoured in its Black History Month programming.

UNB Art Centre

9 · Still unproven — where the hunt goes next

For your own digging, these are the open questions the research leaves honestly on the table:

  • A live, surname-by-surname check of the LAC Collection search and the Nova Scotia Archives Book of Negroes search — including the variant spellings Eastman, Easmon, and Edman, and first-name-only searching for the ~800 entrants with no recorded surname — was not completed. That is the single biggest gap behind the “no Eatmon found” answer.
  • Rose Goseman’s own entry in the Book of Negroes was not individually located — only John’s (item 905) and Fanney’s (item 907) were verified.
  • Fanney’s age: LAC lists her as 1 year old; secondary sources say five months. Spelling also differs (Gozeman vs Goseman).
  • Chester’s death date: 21 July 1988 (MyNewBrunswick) vs 25 July 1988 (WikiTree).
  • Elm Hill’s founding date: 1806 (Wikipedia / genealogy post) vs “about 1812” (Provincial Archives of NB).
  • Descent from a specific named Black Loyalist — for example through Elm Hill founders, or through the McIntyre / Radcliffe / Bowles intermarriages — is unproven. Settling it would need Elm Hill land-grant and muster-roll research, which was not done here.
  • The specific “Chester in the news” story you mentioned was not found. The candidates are the Sep 2025 Facebook tribute, the Jan 2024 UNB exhibit, the Jan 2026 raceway blog — or a mix-up with the July 2026 Christopher Isaiah Eatmon acquittal. An outlet or date would crack it.
  • No portrait of Anne Eatmon was found in the sources searched.
  • Military loose ends (§6), after the follow-up pass: Manzer’s birth date and LAC box and James’s LAC box are now found, and Dubert has a second source. Still open: Arthur’s exact place of death and campaign-medal entitlement and the 3 vs 7 Sep 1939 enlistment date (his file, RG 24 Vol. 25803 Item 10283, was identified but not opened); Mansfield Eatmon’s and Joseph Eatmon’s attestation details; Harry Ellis Eatman’s second source; whether Arthur’s name is on the Fredericton Cenotaph’s Second World War plaque; and Korea service, which public records can neither confirm nor rule out (post-1945 files are ATIP-only).
  • Your tree’s older Eatmons rest on thin sourcing (§7): John Debois Eatmon and Simon Lomax Eatmon carry only “Unsourced Citation” entries, with conflicting spouse names in the hints, and the tree holds two conflicting entries for William B Eatmon (“William B” vs “William Bakman,” 1847–1920). Simon Lomax Eatmon, b. 1800, is where the documented line currently stops — one generation short of the Loyalist era.
  • The shared ancestors behind your two key DNA matches are unnamed (§7): neither Otis Eatmon (141 cM) nor DANIEL Gosman (48 cM) has a named common ancestor in the account — their tree previews are membership-locked or blurred, and DANIEL’s “common ancestors found” detail is locked. Unlocking those trees is the fastest route to testing both connections.
  • The Duke-as-cousin link (§7): James Wallace Eatman as a son of Major Eatmon — making Sgt Arthur “Duke” Eatman your 2nd cousin twice removed — rests on a Find a Grave hint and Major’s contributor-written Find a Grave bio. A primary record for James’s parentage would settle it.
  • Tree data-quality flags (§7): “James Eatmen” is a mis-entered duplicate of Tamar Hopewell, not a separate ancestor; Rosella McIntyre’s death year conflicts (1946 vs abt 1964); Ella M. Eatmon is a daughter in the 1911 census index but a daughter-in-law in Major’s Find a Grave bio; William McIntyre’s birth year conflicts (1841 vs 1835); and William B’s parents conflict between his marriage certificate (“John & Betsy Eatman”) and Find a Grave (mother Tamar Hopewell). All await reconciliation against primary records.
  • Locked behind Ancestry membership (§7): all 63 member photos, all 10 stories, all 77 member trees, and the Otis Eatmon / DANIEL Gosman tree previews were not read — including whether Chester’s wife “Bessie” in the 1986 Windsor Star story (§4) was a second marriage, which remains unverified.
